Basal oxygen consumption in the Western rock elephant shrew has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, yielding a maximum resting metabolic rate of 53.17 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 53.17 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when individuals were measured at their typical active body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This rate, likely recorded during respirometry trials near the thermoneutral zone, provides a key metabolic benchmark for comparing this species with other members of the Macroscelididae. Such a comparatively modest oxygen uptake aligns with the animal's small size and its occupation of rocky, arid habitats in southern Africa, where energy conservation is often at a premium. The measurement underscores how basal expenditure scales with body mass among insectivorous mammals inhabiting climatically harsh environments. Further comparative studies would help clarify whether this value represents an adaptation to the species' specific microhabitat or is largely a consequence of its phylogenetic position within the elephant shrew radiation.

Reproductive data for this species, while limited, indicate that females produce litters containing between 1 and 2 pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = between 1 and 2 pups per reproductive event], with a frequency of approximately 1.5 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters each year], which corresponds to a maximum reproduction rate of 3 pups per year [Ri = 3 pups per year]. This annual output, occurring at a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], resembles the modest fecundity reported for several congeneric species inhabiting similar semi-arid environments. The combination of small litter size and relatively few reproductive bouts per annum suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward high per-offspring investment rather than maximizing numerical output. Such a pattern is typical of small mammals that face unpredictable resource availability, where producing a smaller number of more robust young may enhance survival during periods of scarcity.

Neonatal individuals of the Western rock elephant shrew emerge at a wet body mass of 15.5 grams [Wwb = 15.5 grams], a value estimated from closely related forms and representing the delicate stage at which newborns begin their extrauterine development. Adult females ultimately attain a substantially larger asymptotic body mass, with the upper end of the reported range reaching 65 grams [Wwi = 65 grams], though individual variation is considerable and the species' female ultimate wet weight likely spans from approximately 44 to 65 grams. This dramatic increase from birth to maturity underscores the substantial nutritional demands placed on both the neonate for growth and the lactating female for milk production. The trajectory of mass gain across development highlights the energetic challenge of reaching reproductive size in a landscape where insect prey may be patchily distributed.

Longevity records for this species, inferred from data on the closely related Elephantulus intufi, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 4.2 years [am = approximately 4.2 years] under conditions where a stable core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] is maintained. Such a lifespan positions the Western rock elephant shrew among the longer-lived small insectivores, a pattern often associated with reduced extrinsic mortality in rocky refugia. The gestation period, also estimated from congeneric data, lasts 51 days [tg = 51 days] at a maternal temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], a length of pregnancy that is protracted relative to that of many rodents of similar body mass. This extended developmental interval likely facilitates the birth of relatively precocial young that are better equipped to navigate the rocky terrain soon after parturition.

The developmental schedule continues with weaning, which occurs at 28 days after birth [tx = 28 days after birth] when the mother maintains a body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], meaning the nursing pups transition to solid food relatively early compared to some other afrotherian mammals. Puberty, conversely, is not attained until approximately 330 days after birth [tp = approximately 330 days after birth], with this milestone recorded at a slightly lower body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], possibly reflecting a nocturnal or inactive metabolic state. The prolonged period between weaning and the onset of reproductive capability implies a lengthy juvenile and sub-adult phase during which individuals must refine foraging skills, establish home ranges, and accumulate sufficient body reserves. This slow pace of maturation, combined with a modest reproductive rate and an extended lifespan, paints a portrait of a species finely tuned to the constraints of a stable but resource-limited environment.
